Why fiscal injection uses a proxy

Monthly FGN recurrent spending, the basis of the Fiscal Injection Index, has not been published since December 2024. FAAC distributions (CBN distributable pool to 2024, then the amount shared reported by the Office of the Accountant-General) are the closest monthly fiscal flow still released. Over 2010–2024 their growth moved only loosely with recurrent spending (correlation about 0.2–0.4), so read the proxy as the direction of fiscal flows, not as the index itself. In past cycles the Fiscal Injection Index rose ahead of the vote in — of — cycles, by — more than in normal times.

Model projection against an election-pressure scenario

The model projects inflation easing further because it extends the disinflation since early 2025 and estimates a small, uncertain election effect. It cannot see fuel-price or tariff changes, a reversal of the naira, or spending pushed through after the vote. The scenario asks a simpler question: starting from the latest published month, what happens if 2027 repeats what each past election did from the same point of its cycle? It is a guide to risk, not a forecast.

Indicator and monthModel projection (median)Scenario: past-cycle averageRange across past cycles

Six cycles, 2003–2023. In 2015 and 2023 the naira was devalued or unified after the vote, which sets the high end for the exchange rate; 2003 sets the high end for inflation.

Does inflation rise after the vote? Testing the specification

  • The paper's single election index runs from six months before the vote to two months after and fades out. With one coefficient it can only describe an effect that starts at once and dies away, so it attributes the pre-vote dip in inflation to elections and leaves the post-vote rise to other shocks.
  • The test version splits it: a pre-vote index (the same ramp up to the vote) and a post-vote index for the six months after. Six months fitted best of three, six, nine and twelve.
  • With the post-vote index, the election effect on inflation turns from a dip at the vote to roughly zero or slightly positive six months later, and the naira effect lasts longer. The direction supports a post-election catch-up, but the post-vote coefficient is small and imprecisely estimated, and standard fit criteria do not prefer the test version over the paper's.
  • The June 2023 exchange-rate regime dummy coincides with the 2023 post-vote months and absorbs much of that cycle's inflation surge. Without it the post-vote effect is larger (inflation and the naira both), but the model fits worse because the dummy also captures the lasting post-2023 regime.
  • Reading: elections hold inflation down before the vote (frozen fuel prices and tariffs, a defended naira) and some of it returns afterwards. How much of the post-vote rise is an election effect, rather than one-off reforms timed after the vote, the data cannot yet separate.

Four ways of estimating the same model

Chosen specification and spending, with 90% ranges. The methods agree on where inflation and the naira are heading; they differ on the size of the election effect, and in every Bayesian version its range includes zero. The standard VARX shows no range for the effect because it treats the coefficients as known.

How the projection is built

  1. The model is the paper's VARX: inflation, naira depreciation, fiscal and liquidity injection, with election regressors and exchange-rate regime dummies, one lag, estimated on 2000–2024. The paper's specification uses the single Election Spending Index; the test version uses separate pre-vote and post-vote indices.
  2. It is estimated four ways. Stochastic volatility (bsvars) lets shock sizes change over time, so the calmer 2025–26 period is not judged by 2023–24 turbulence; it is the default. A hierarchical Minnesota prior (bsvarSIGNs) lets the data choose how much to shrink coefficients. Constant volatility (bsvars) is the plain Bayesian version. The standard VARX is the least-squares estimate. Each Bayesian model keeps 1,000 draws from 7,000 iterations.
  3. For every draw the forecast starts in December 2024, the last month with fiscal data, and is forced to match every published month of inflation, depreciation and the Liquidity Injection Index since. The fiscal index after 2024 is inferred, not observed.
  4. The election effect holds every other shock fixed, as in the paper's counterfactual. The spending choice scales the part of the election effect still to come: in the test version that includes the post-vote index.
  5. The 2023 and 2024 regime dummies were fitted on the unification and float, so left alone they pull the projection back towards 2023–24 devaluation rates. Each draw instead carries forward the average shock of its last twelve observed months (an intercept correction), assuming the post-2024 pattern continues. The election effect does not depend on this choice.
  6. The model works with year-on-year depreciation, so the projected naira path inherits the month-to-month pattern of a year earlier. Spending is the simulated index, not measured outlays.

Units: inflation in percentage points, exchange rate in percent change of naira per dollar, indices in standard deviations. Run-up covers seven months before the vote to the vote; after covers the vote to six months later.

What sits behind the large cells

  • 2003: the June 2003 increase in pump prices lifted inflation sharply in the months after the vote.
  • 2015: the naira was devalued in November 2014 and February 2015, inside the run-up to the March 2015 vote.
  • 2023: the exchange-rate windows were unified in June 2023, four months after the February vote, and inflation rose through the second half of the year.
  • 2007 and 2019: the naira was held close to its pre-election level in both windows.

These are policy events that coincide with the electoral calendar. The monitor cannot tell whether the election caused them or whether adjustments were timed around the vote; both readings point to the period just after an election as the time of greatest risk.

Government spending, deficit and debt

FGN recurrent and capital spending and the deficit are twelve-month totals from the CBN's monthly FGN finances, which end in December 2024; no monthly series has been published since, and Budget Office implementation reports for 2025–26 are late and partial. Public debt is the Debt Management Office's quarterly stock for the Federal Government, States and FCT, updated automatically.

Response to an election-spending impulse

VARX estimates: inflation, naira depreciation, fiscal and liquidity injection respond to the Election Spending Index, with exchange-rate regime dummies. The impulse raises the index from zero to its peak for one month. Shaded bands are 90% bootstrap intervals; a band that spans zero means the response is not statistically distinguishable from no effect.

How to read this monitor

Election window
Six months before the first general-election vote of each cycle to two months after it. Votes covered: —.
Normal times
The same calendar span anchored on months at least twelve months from any vote (— anchor months). The difference between an election cycle and normal times is the excess change shown on every card.
Verdict
An indicator rises (or eases) in a segment when at least four of the six cycles sit above (or at most two above, with a negative average) the normal-times change.
Election Spending Index (ESI)
A simulated 0–1 profile: rises evenly from six months before the vote, equals 1 in the month before and the month of the vote, then 0.5 and 0.25 in the two months after.
Fiscal Injection Index (FII)
Standardised year-on-year growth of FGN recurrent expenditure (three-month average). Fuel subsidies are excluded because no consistent series exists for 2000–2024.
Fiscal injection, FAAC proxy
Because monthly FGN spending stops in December 2024, the 2027 watch and History use standardised year-on-year growth of FAAC distributions (three-month average): the CBN distributable pool to December 2024, then the amount shared reported by the Office of the Accountant-General. Standardised on 2010–2024. Monitoring only; it moves loosely with recurrent spending (correlation about 0.2–0.4).
Liquidity Injection Index (LII)
Average of standardised M2 growth, net OMO injection and net Treasury bill injection (maturities less new sales over twelve months, as a share of M2).
Model
VARX with lag length chosen by BIC, estimated on 2000–2024; the ESI enters as an exogenous variable with regime dummies for June 2016, June 2023 and February 2024. The counterfactual sets the ESI to zero. Bands come from 500 residual-bootstrap replications.
Data
Central Bank of Nigeria statistical bulletins and data portal (CPI from NBS; fiscal data from the Office of the Accountant-General). Fiscal series before 2010 are interpolated from annual totals.

Limits of the evidence

  • Six elections are a small sample; a single cycle (2003 inflation, 2015 and 2023 exchange rate) can move the average.
  • The ESI is simulated from the electoral calendar, not measured spending, so the model captures what typically happens around elections rather than spending itself.
  • Fiscal data for 2022–2024 are provisional, and pre-2010 monthly fiscal values are interpolated.
  • The official exchange rate is used throughout the analysis; parallel-market pressure before 2023 is not captured. The BDC rate on the 2027 watch comes from a hand-compiled daily workbook and is shown for monitoring only. Year-on-year depreciation lags turns by up to a year, so the monitor also shows month-on-month changes and the daily rate.
  • The election-pressure scenario on the Projection tab replays what each past cycle did from the same point; it inherits one-off events such as the 2015 and 2023 exchange-rate adjustments and is a guide to risk, not a forecast.

Sources: Central Bank of Nigeria Annual and Quarterly Statistical Bulletins and CBN data portal (consumer prices from the National Bureau of Statistics; fiscal data from the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation). Election dates from INEC.

Estimates: event study against normal times and VARX structural counterfactual, monthly data 2000–2024, estimated in Python and replicated in R. Standalone copy generated 13 November 2026; it works offline and contains all data shown.
